column4: The two boys are explicitly يَتِيمَيْنِ; their righteous father's treasure is preserved until they reach maturity, and رَبُّكَ wills that growth as mercy, gathering orphanhood, guardianship, maturation, and the Lord in one scene.
Mary's Lord gives her good growth, entrusts her to Zechariah, and he finds provision beside her; this directly joins the section's stage-by-stage raising, foster guardian, finding, and provision.
Moses' sister offers an أَهْلِ بَيْتٍ who will undertake his care and sincerely look after him, an exact Quranic household for the section's received child.
God returns the separated infant to his mother so that her eye may be comforted and she not grieve; the sheltering household repairs a broken parent-child bond.
Pharaoh's أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا matches the remembered-care question and the source dictionary's raising of a child, but makes the foster household itself the speaker.
Moses exposes the supposed foster “favor” as inseparable from enslaving Israel; it is the section's direct counter-scene to divine care that becomes care for others rather than a debt.
The Egyptian tells his wife to honor Joseph's lodging and considers taking him as a son, a direct scene of a displaced boy being received into a home.

The community is recalled as few and made weak, after which God shelters them, strengthens them, and provides good things; it expands the orphan's sequence from vulnerability to shelter and provision.
The ruling on ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ says that setting their affairs right is best and that sharing life with them makes them “your brothers,” directly opening the household to the orphan.

Guardians test the orphans until marriageable age and sound judgment, then return their property; the verse also distinguishes a rich guardian from a poor one who may take fairly, exactly joining maturation with the poor provider.
The grown child asks for mercy on the parents كَمَا رَبَّيَانِى صَغِيرًا; the source's raising verb and softened heart become a precise reversal of care received in childhood.

Mothers nurse to completion while the father must provide food and clothing according to fairness, and neither parent is harmed through the child; this spells out the household's shared work of raising.
The verse commands lodging women where one lives, support through pregnancy, payment for nursing, and fair consultation, making shelter and infant care concrete household duties.

A person of restricted provision must still spend from what God has given, and God promises ease after hardship; this directly illuminates the section's poor person who nevertheless maintains dependents.
The infant Moses is cast where an enemy household will take him, while God places love on him and has him formed “under My eye”; hostile surroundings become divine nurture.
Moses' sister leads to someone who will care for him, and he is returned to his mother before God brings him through successive trials; separation, foster care, reunion, and formation all meet here.
Pharaoh's wife forbids killing the found infant and proposes taking him as a son, turning the persecutor's house, provisionally, into refuge.
God tells Moses' mother to nurse him, promises to return him, and answers her fear at the moment she must release him; divine guardianship holds the broken household together.
The casting of pens decides which man will sponsor Mary, showing that a child without her father requires a particular guardian rather than an abstract kindness.

The verse names foster mothers and sisters through nursing and رَبَائِبُكُمُ ٱلَّٰتِى فِى حُجُورِكُمْ; it supplies the Quranic family-law boundary for the source dictionary's child raised in another's lap.
Joseph ءَاوَىٰٓ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ, drawing his brother into his own protected space and beginning the family's return to him.
Joseph ءَاوَىٰٓ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ and welcomes the family into safety, reversing his own childhood reception into care for his parents.
The people settled in the home love those who migrate to them and prefer them despite their own privation; it is a communal version of the poor household that shelters and provides.
The command to marry the unmarried says that if they are poor God will enrich them, directly realizing the source dictionary's connection between غِنَى and marriage.
Those unable to find means for marriage remain chaste until God enriches them; marriage and enrichment are again held together, now across a period of waiting.
Spouses are created so that one may dwell in tranquility with the other, with affection and mercy placed between them; this gives Quranic substance to marriage as a sheltering fortress.
Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision appear in one divine gift, closely matching the section's house enlarged through marriage and sustained by provision.
Mary and her son are made a sign and given refuge on secure high ground with flowing water, an explicit mother-child shelter joined to provision.
Those who gave refuge and aid to emigrants become their protecting allies; shelter creates a relation of mutual responsibility like the section's enlarged household.
The believers who migrated and those who sheltered and helped them are declared true believers, making reception of the vulnerable a defining bond.
The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord for mercy and sound direction, linking physical shelter with the Lord's compassionate guidance.
The youths are told to seek refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease in their affair; a non-house becomes the sheltering household of the image.
رَبَّ هَٰذَا ٱلْبَيْتِ names the Lord of the House, giving a Quranic meeting for the source dictionary's “owner of the house” while retaining the divine Lord.
Linked to 106:3's Lord of the House, this ayah says He feeds against hunger and secures against fear, the two basic acts of the sheltering, provisioning home.
The covenant joins good treatment of parents and kin with ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ and the needy, placing the orphan inside the community's closest obligations.
Righteousness includes giving cherished wealth to kin, ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ, the needy, and travelers; the home opened to the orphan becomes a test of substantive piety.
The answer about spending names parents, relatives, ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ, the needy, and travelers, specifying where the recipient of provision must redirect what is given.
The orphan's property must be handed over intact rather than absorbed into the guardian's wealth, setting a concrete boundary on the power of the receiving household.
Fear of injustice toward orphan girls governs whom and how many one may marry; the verse makes marriage inside an orphan-managing household answerable to justice.
When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, they are to receive something and be addressed kindly, joining material care to non-humiliating speech.
The command to worship God is immediately embodied in goodness to parents, kin, ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ, the needy, neighbors, companions, and travelers.
The ruling names orphan women whose prescribed rights are withheld in the very context of desired marriage, and commands justice for orphans.
One may approach the orphan's property only in the best manner until maturity, defining care as preservation across the child's growth.
A fixed share of spoils is assigned to ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ and the needy, turning care of the fatherless into a public claim on communal wealth.
The orphan's property is protected until maturity, matching both the source definition's pre-puberty limit and the household's duty to bring the child safely to completion.
Fay is directed to ٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ and the needy so that wealth does not merely circulate among the rich, making household care part of a wider distributive order.
The righteous feed the needy, the orphan, and the captive despite their own desire for the food, enacting provision from a household that may itself have little.
The difficult ascent includes feeding يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ, an orphan who is also kin, so the vulnerable child is explicitly within the family circle.
Guardians are told to imagine leaving weak offspring behind, fear for them, and speak rightly; the command makes another's vulnerable child feel like one's own.
When a debtor is weak or unable to dictate, the guardian must dictate justly, giving the section's dependent weak person a concrete supporter and voice.
Oppressed men, women, and children ask God for a protecting ally and helper, turning the section's vulnerable child and supporting household into a communal rescue imperative.
The truly weakened men, women, and children cannot devise a plan or يَهْتَدُونَ سَبِيلًا, a close Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's weak person unable to proceed without support.
“Our Lord” gives each thing its created form and then guides it; giving, guidance, and stage-wise fitting meet in one account of divine nurture.
The addressee must command his household to prayer and persevere, while God says “We provide for you”; household responsibility rests on divine provision rather than abundance in the provider.
Household servants and children below puberty must ask permission at three private times, giving the growing child a defined place and duty within the home.
Once the household's children reach puberty they ask permission like adults, marking the same maturation boundary built into the source definition of orphanhood.
The blind, lame, and sick are explicitly free to eat in a wide network of family houses, and people may eat together; weakness is included rather than shut outside the home.
Young attendants circulate among the household “like hidden pearls”; the verse uniquely meets both source dictionary details of the serving boy and the child figured as a precious pearl.
Everlasting youths circulate in service and appear like scattered pearls, again joining the section's child who hands the household what it wants with its “orphan pearl” valuation.
Moses waters for the two women and then admits his own need for whatever good God sends; the needy outsider first serves a vulnerable household and then is received by it.
One woman comes to Moses and leads him to her father, who tells him he is safe; guidance, a softened response, and entry into a protective home converge.
The father offers Moses marriage to a daughter in exchange for years of service, forming a household around a displaced poor man through marriage and work.
The mother's weakness upon weakness and two years of weaning specify the labor by which a child is raised and ground the child's later gratitude.
Pregnancy, birth, nursing, maturity, and the adult's prayer for parents and offspring trace care across stages and generations, closely matching growth toward completion.
Believers must guard both themselves and their families from the Fire, stating the householder's protective responsibility at its widest boundary.
Linked to 76:8's feeding of the orphan, the carers seek neither repayment nor thanks; their care directly reverses Pharaoh's use of upbringing as a claim against Moses.
This ayah supplies the act governing 90:15: feeding on a day of hunger, so care for the kin-orphan is costly provision rather than a sentiment.
After the feeding of the orphan and destitute in 90:14-16, believers counsel one another to mercy, naming the softened heart that sustains the section's household.
The question “Have you seen the one who denies the Judgment?” is answered by 107:2's treatment of the orphan, paralleling the section's use of a question to expose what remembered care must produce.
Beside 107:2's repulsion of the orphan, failure to urge feeding the poor joins the two vulnerable figures that 93:6-9 places in one moral sequence.
The human being reads the Lord's generous provision as personal honor; 89:17 then tests that claim by whether the orphan is honored, linking received bounty to household conduct.
Following 89:17's failure to honor the orphan, people also fail to urge feeding the needy; the closed door affects both the fatherless child and the poor.
The Godfearing person gives wealth to purify himself, supplying the active generosity toward which the recipient of divine care is turned.
Linked to 92:18's giving, no one's favor is being repaid; this is the clean opposite of Pharaoh converting foster care into an outstanding debt.
The giver “will surely be satisfied,” echoing 93:5's promise of satisfaction while showing the satisfaction alongside generous care rather than possession.
The same addressee is met with another intimate “Have We not?” reminder of divine care, this time the opening of his breast; it reinforces the stance of 93:6 without replacing its orphan scene.
After Joseph is received into the Egyptian home in 12:21, this ayah brings him to full maturity and gives him judgment and knowledge, completing the fostered child's growth.
In the house that received him, Joseph says his rabb has made his lodging good; whether rabb here is read as God or master, the wording activates the source's meeting of Lord and householder.
After 12:99's reception of his parents, Joseph raises them to the throne and names God's subtle care through the family's reunion, completing the formerly displaced child's reversal of role.
After Moses' foster-household story, reaching full strength brings wisdom and knowledge; it is the completed-growth endpoint implicit in the source dictionary's tarbiya.
The two women hold back from the well because their father is old; this supplies the weak household whose need Moses answers in 28:24-27.
The daughter asks her father to hire Moses as strong and trustworthy, turning the outsider's help into sustained service within the household formed in 28:27.
Spouses are “clothing” for one another, a reciprocal image of covering and closeness that makes concrete the source dictionary's marriage-as-fortress sense.
A believer without means to marry a free woman may marry a believing bondwoman through her people and with a proper dower; the verse treats marriage as guarded belonging available amid poverty.
The mate is created from the same soul so that one may find rest with her, and the pair then carry a child; the ayah shows a household beginning in shelter and growing.
The prayer asks that spouses and offspring become comfort to the eyes, presenting the enlarged household as a gift requiring righteous formation.
God grants daughters or sons as He wills, placing the house's growth under divine giving rather than human possession.
Paired sons and daughters or childlessness complete 42:49's account, marking the limits around how a household grows.
The verse grounds responsibility for household maintenance in expenditure from one's wealth, a specific Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's person who supports dependents.
Ishmael commands his household to prayer and almsgiving, portraying a family member actively tending the house's moral and material obligations.
Human beings are the poor in relation to God while God is ٱلْغَنِىُّ; this theological dependence clarifies why even the householder who provides remains one sustained by the Lord.
Human creation is narrated through successive bodily states until maturity, a direct Quranic analogue for the source dictionary's raising “state by state to completion.”
The human being is brought from created stages to infancy, full strength, and old age, extending the section's child-growth image across an entire life.
God creates from weakness, gives strength, and returns strength to weakness; the sequence illuminates why the household's supporting roles eventually reverse.
God has created people in stages, succinctly stating the staged formation that the source dictionary places inside the meaning of raising.
Moses asks for a helper “from my family,” locating needed support inside kinship rather than solitary strength.
The requested brother is to strengthen Moses' back, a nonlexical Quranic counterpart to the source's weak person proceeding by leaning on others.
God promises to strengthen Moses' arm through his brother, making family support the answer to confessed weakness.
Even a hostile outsider who asks protection must be granted refuge and then conveyed to safety; shelter here creates a temporary duty toward a vulnerable stranger.
Unable to protect his guests, Lot wishes for strength or a powerful refuge; the scene exposes what a householder needs in order to shelter those who enter his home.
Everlasting youths circulate in service, corresponding to the source dictionary's child working within the household.
The cups, pitchers, and drink carried by the youths of 56:17 specify the things they place into others' hands, completing that secondary dictionary scene.
Spending is not to be followed by reminders of generosity or injury, a precise ethical boundary between sheltering care and Pharaoh's weaponized recollection of nurture.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, showing that provision which humiliates the recipient contradicts the house's softened heart.
Believers must not nullify charity through reminders and harm; this gives the explicit rule violated when Pharaoh presents childhood care as leverage.
The addressee is told not to confer favor seeking increase, reinforcing the section's distinction between a divine gift that opens the hand and a favor used as a claim.
Linked to 92:18-19, the giver seeks only the face of the Most High Lord, locating care's motive outside household status or repayment.
Within the orphan-property passage, those not ready to manage wealth are still to be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly from it; guardianship joins preservation with daily care.
Alongside the kin-orphan of 90:15 stands a destitute person in misery, echoing the section's movement from orphanhood to poverty within one field of care.
Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly consume fire into themselves; this is the receiving household transformed from guardian into predator.
Restricted provision is misread as the Lord's humiliation, but 89:17 immediately redirects attention to humans who fail to honor the orphan; poverty itself is not the disgrace.
لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ names the house that withholds honor, the explicit reverse of sheltering the child and refusing to humiliate him.
The denier يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ, violently pushing away the very child whom the section's house takes in.
Pharaoh's policy slaughters sons and weakens their people; it supplies the violent household background against which his family receives Moses in 28:8-9.
After citing Moses' upbringing in 26:18, Pharaoh calls him ungrateful; the ayah shows exactly how recalled care is converted into moral coercion.
Noah calls his son to board with the family, but the son remains apart; a father's offered refuge can be refused.
Noah's son says he will take refuge on a mountain, but no protector exists that day except divine mercy; physical shelter without the Lord reaches its limit.
Noah appeals that his son is of his household, bringing the claim of family belonging before God after the failed rescue.
God says the son is not of Noah's household because his conduct is unrighteous, setting a severe boundary on biological belonging as shelter.
God has not made adopted sons biological sons; the verse preserves a legal boundary even while the section dignifies raising another's child.
Adopted children are called by their fathers, and those whose fathers are unknown remain brothers in faith and protected associates; lost paternity does not erase belonging, but its form is defined.
The former wife of an adopted son is not treated by the law as a biological son's wife, a marriage boundary around the foster relation developed in the section.
If spouses separate, God can enrich each from His abundance; the ayah bounds the source dictionary's marriage–غِنَى link by showing divine enrichment also beyond marriage.
Children must not be killed for fear of poverty because God provides for them and their parents; imagined scarcity cannot close the household against its child.
Children must not be killed from poverty, for God provides for parent and child; it reverses the section's poor provider into the false claim that poverty cancels care.
The buried girl is summoned as a speaking party on Judgment Day, restoring standing to the child whom a household cast out of life.
Her question asks for what sin she was killed, exposing the furthest possible opposite of receiving and raising a vulnerable child.
No parent can avail a child nor a child a parent on the final day, setting the eschatological limit of the household's mutual support.
The wives of Noah and Lot live under righteous husbands yet the household bond cannot protect them from God, another boundary on family as ultimate refuge.
Pharaoh's wife asks God for a house near Him and rescue from Pharaoh, replacing an oppressive earthly household with divine refuge.
The sinner would ransom himself with his sons, reversing the householder's duty to protect children into sacrificing them for himself.
Spouse and brother are added to the family members the sinner would surrender, undoing the mutual return that defines the source's household.
He would even ransom the clan ٱلَّتِى تُـْٔوِيهِ, the very family that used to shelter him; received refuge is betrayed rather than repaid through care.
Joseph asks whether many lords are better than God, the One, the Subduer; house-masters and ٱلْقَهَّارُ meet here to reserve ultimate qahr for God, unlike human humiliation of an orphan.
The human being transgresses, with 96:7 identifying the trigger as imagined self-sufficiency; enrichment that forgets dependence produces the opposite of the section's commanded care.
أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ makes self-perceived independence the cause of tyranny, a pointed reversal of being enriched by the Lord and then protecting the vulnerable.

The source dictionary explicitly calls the rare solitary thing a “unique pearl”; the ayah's singular كَوْكَبٌ دُرِّىٌّ may therefore echo that secondary valuation, though it describes a radiant star rather than a child.
